rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prohibitions can honor what is sacred or debase what is forbidden; place, time, lineage, nursing, and affinity prohibitions carry sanctity, while immoralities, carrion, blood, and wine are degraded.
rows.anchor: فتحريم المكان والزمان مزية وتفضيل ، وتحريم الفواحش والميتة والدم والخمر تحقير لها ، والمحرمات للنسل والرضاع والصهر زيادة في الحرمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A sacred place bars what harms its condition, and sacred time such as the forbidden months bars what harms those living in it.
rows.anchor: فتحريم المكان : منع ما يضر بالحال فيه . وتحريم الزمان ، كتحريم الأشهر الحرم : منع ما فيه ضر للموجودين فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saying that God owns everything guards against thinking that describing Him as Lord of the town limits His sovereignty to it; the addition honors the town.
rows.anchor: ليعلم أن تلك الإضافة لتشريف المضاف إليه لا لتعريف المضاف بتعيين مظهر ملكه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating “I was commanded” distinguishes Moses’ private, inspired command, by which God had kept him from idolatry before revelation, from his prophetic command to call people to monotheism.
rows.anchor: للإشارة إلى الاختلاف بين الأمرين فإن الأول أمر يعمله في خاصة نفسه وهو أمر إلهام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second command entails the prophetic mission and calling people to monotheism.
rows.anchor: والأمر الثاني أمر يقتضي الرسالة وقد شمل دعوة الخلق إلى التوحيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “I was commanded” is not repeated before reciting the Qur’an because Islam and recitation are both aspects of the prophetic mission.
rows.anchor: لأن كلا من الإسلام والتلاوة من شؤون الرسالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling himself one of the Muslims honors this community, since God made His Messenger one of its members.
rows.anchor: تنويه بهذه الأمة إذ جعل الله رسوله من آحادها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tilāwa means reading a specified text to people; Ibn ʿĀshūr links the usage to earlier Qur’anic instances.
rows.anchor: قراءة كلام معين على الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The object of recitation is omitted because it is obvious: the Prophet is to recite the Qur’an to people.
rows.anchor: أي أن أتلوا القرآن على الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Recitation divides people into those guided and those who do not benefit; guidance benefits the guided person, which encourages listeners to follow the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: مبينا أن من اهتدى فإنما كان اهتداؤه لفائدة نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Explicitly saying “say” stresses that the Prophet’s duty toward those who turn away is to deliver warning, not to let their rejection draw him into pressing them to accept.
rows.anchor: أن يبلغهم الإنذار فلا يطمعوا أن يحمله إعراضهم على أن يلح عليهم قبول دعوته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warners are the messengers: Muhammad is one of them, not a novel messenger, and their practice is simply to convey the message.
rows.anchor: ما كنت بدعا من الرسل وسنتي سنة من أرسل من الرسل قبلي وهي التبليغ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After recounting guidance, revelation, and the prophetic mission as great blessings, God commands praise with the comprehensive formula He uses of Himself.
rows.anchor: من أعظم النعم عليه في الدنيا وأبشرها بأعظم درجة في الآخرة من أجل ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The close guards against opponents inferring from the Prophet’s disavowal of unseen knowledge and limited mission that the threatened punishment will fail; the threat is near and certain.
rows.anchor: فتظهر لهم دلائل صدق الله في وعده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the threatened punishment “signs” indicates that events will confirm what the Messenger warned them about.
rows.anchor: ولذلك عبر عن الوعيد بالآيات إشارة إلى أنهم سيحل بهم ما فيه تصديق لما أخبرهم به الرسول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Recognizing the signs means recognizing how they point to the warning delivered by the Messenger.
rows.anchor: تعرفون دلالتها على ما بلغكم الرسول من النذارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The future particle signals near manifestation: worldly signs include smoke, the moon’s splitting, and the chiefs’ destruction at Badr, recognized as they occur or even at death’s agony.
rows.anchor: فالآيات حاصلة في الدنيا مثل الدخان

rows.speaker: أبو سفيان
rows.claim: On the night of the conquest, Abu Sufyan said he knew that if another god existed alongside God, it would have helped him.
rows.anchor: لقد علمت أن لو كان مع الله إله غيره لقد أغنى عني شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise of signs also connects to the signs in the horizons and within people that disclose the truth.
rows.anchor: حتى يتبين لهم أنه الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One sign within them was believers’ swords striking the chiefs who had oppressed them at Badr.
rows.anchor: فمن الآيات في أنفسهم إعمال سيوف المؤمنين الذين كانوا يستضعفونهم في أعناق سادتهم وكبرائهم يوم بدر

rows.speaker: أبو جهل
rows.claim: As he lay dying at Badr, Abu Jahl asked who could be more helpless than a man killed by his own people, referring to himself; this outcome had never occurred to him.
rows.anchor: يعني نفسه وهو ما لم يكن يخطر له على بال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥafṣ, Abū Jaʿfar, and Yaʿqūb read the verb with second-person tāʾ, making the warning part of what the Prophet is told to say to the polytheists.
rows.anchor: قرأه نافع وابن عامر وحفص وأبو جعفر ويعقوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This direct address adds a threat: their conduct in receiving Muhammad’s message merits the signs, and God is watching them.
rows.anchor: وفيه زيادة إنذار بأن أعمالهم تستوجب ما سيرونه من الآيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The remaining readers use third-person yāʾ; this coordinates with “say” and consoles the Prophet that God has recorded their deeds and will requite them, so he should not despair of divine aid.
rows.anchor: والمقصود تسلية الرسول عليه السلام بعدما أمر به من القول بأن الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah ends with a comprehensive and supremely eloquent conclusion.
rows.anchor: وقد جاءت خاتمة جامعة بالغة أقصى حد من بلاغة حسن الختام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story omits many intervening events: Moses grew up in Pharaoh’s palace and was counted among Pharaoh’s household.
rows.anchor: طويت أخبار كثيرة تنبىء عنها القصة وذلك أن موسى يفع وشب في قصر فرعون فكان معدودا من أهل بيت فرعون

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One reported account says Moses was called the son of Pharaoh.
rows.anchor: كان يدعى موسى ابن فرعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The entry into the city continues the episode of God’s instruction to Moses’ mother to nurse him; Moses may have learned his origin from her visits and account of his story.
rows.anchor: عطف جزء القصة على جزء آخر منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The city is Memphis, the northern Egyptian capital.
rows.anchor: هي ( منفيس ) قاعدة مصر الشمالية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “At a time of heedlessness” attaches grammatically to “entered”; the preposition “on” is metaphorical elevation, like “upon guidance,” meaning he was secure during a heedless interval.
rows.anchor: أي متمكنا من حين غفلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heedless time was when people rested, dispersed, and left the roads empty.
rows.anchor: وهو وقت استراحة الناس وتفرقهم وخلو الطريق منهم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some say it was at midday, with Moses crossing the city alone; another report says he was going to catch up with Pharaoh, who had passed through it.
rows.anchor: قيل : كان ذلك في وقت القيلولة وكان موسى مجتازا بالمدينة وحده ، قيل ليلحق بفرعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning the hour signals that no one witnessed the Egyptian’s killing, preparing for the accusation in verse 19 and the account of Moses’ departure from Egypt.
rows.anchor: الإشارة إلى أن قتله القبطي لم يشعر به أحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two demonstratives unpack the otherwise general statement that two men were fighting.
rows.anchor: تفصيل لما أجمل في قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic demonstratives here need not distinguish near from far: they may match, as here and in 4:143, or differ, as in al-Mutalammis’ poem.
rows.anchor: فلذلك قد تكون الإشارتان متماثلتين كما هنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A shiʿa is a group affiliated with someone, as in 28:4; an enemy is the group Moses opposed, the Israelites’ adversaries among Pharaoh’s Copts.
rows.anchor: والشيعة : الجماعة المنتمية إلى أحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The man from Moses’ group was an Israelite and his enemy an Egyptian; “enemy” can be grammatically singular or plural.
rows.anchor: والعدو وصف يستوي فيه الواحد والجمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses may have known his Israelite identity through his mother’s account of his rescue, and so grew to hate the Copts while inwardly loving the Israelites.
rows.anchor: أن موسى كان يعلم أنه من بني إسرائيل بإخبار قصة التقاطه من اليم وأن تكون أمه قد أفضت إليه بخبرها وخبره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On either account, Moses’ blow against the Copt was an effort to uphold right; when the later dispute arose, the Copt accused him of tyranny rather than favoritism toward his people.
rows.anchor: وأما وكزه القبطي فلم يكن إلا انتصارا للحق على جميع التقادير

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One report says the Copt worked in Pharaoh’s bakery, asked an Israelite to carry wood to the oven, and tried to force him when he refused, producing a severe fight.
rows.anchor: قيل : كان القبطي من عملة مخبز فرعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Fighting” is metaphorical here for their severe beating of one another.
rows.anchor: فاختصما وتضاربا ضربا شديدا وهو المعبر عنه بالتقاتل على طريق الاستعارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Appealing for help means asking to be rescued from distress or helped against hardship; the call implies the Israelite was overpowered and the Copt unjustly forced labor on him.
rows.anchor: فذكر الاستغاثة يؤذن بأن الإسرائيلي كان مغلوبا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Copt was the aggressor because nobody may be compelled to do work against his will.
rows.anchor: وكان ظالما إذ لا يجبر أحد على عمل يعمله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A wakz is a blow with the hand, fingers gathered as in making the form of a seventy-three knot.
rows.anchor: الضرب باليد بجمع أصابعها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This gathering of the fingers is called al-jamʿ, with ḍamma on jīm and sukūn on mīm.
rows.anchor: ويسمى الجمع بضم الجيم وسكون الميم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “He finished him” is a fixed idiom for death, with an omitted agent understood as death decreeing it; Moses’ blow therefore killed the Copt.
rows.anchor: بمعنى مات لا تغير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the pronoun may refer to God, the only one who decrees death, as in 34:14.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون عائدا إلى الله تعالى المفهوم من المقام إذ لا يقضي بالموت غيره

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some take the pronoun in “he finished him” to refer to Moses, but Ibn ʿĀshūr says that reading is not evident.
rows.anchor: عائد إلى موسى وليس هذا بالبين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses did not intend to kill the Egyptian; his blow accidentally struck a vital point and killed him.
rows.anchor: وكان هذا قتل خطأ صادف الوكز مقاتل القبطي ولم يرد موسى قتله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Torah’s Exodus account says Moses looked around, saw no one, killed the Egyptian, and buried him in sand.
rows.anchor: ووقع في سفر الخروج من التوراة في الإصحاح الثاني أن موسى لما رأى المصري يضرب العبراني التفت هنا وهناك ورأى أن ليس أحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “He said, this is Satan’s work” is an explanatory resumption answering what Moses did on seeing the Copt die; it shows his immediate concern was religious and is self-directed speech.
rows.anchor: ماذا كان من أمر موسى حين فوجىء بموت القبطي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “This” may refer to the excessive blow, the death he saw caused by it, or the anger that led to the death.
rows.anchor: التي تسبب عليها الموت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan inflamed Moses’ anger until his blow became excessive.
rows.anchor: أن الشيطان أوقد غضبه حتى بالغ في شدة الوكز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Killing a protected person is abhorrent in human laws, since preserving inviolable life is foundational to all religions; Moses may have learned his ancestral religion from his mother.
rows.anchor: لأن قتل النفس مستقبح في الشرائع البشرية فإن حفظ النفس المعصومة من أصول الأديان كلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan’s enmity and routes into human minds explain Moses’ excessive anger: without the satanic thought he would have stopped the Copt, and the killing arose from whispering.
rows.anchor: لولا الخاطر الشيطاني لاقتصر على زجر القبطي أو كفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The human soul is originally good and in its natural disposition; deviation from that state requires an external, nonnatural cause such as Satan’s prompting.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا دليل على أن الأصل في النفس الإنسانية هو الخير وأنه الفطرة وأن الانحراف عنها يحتاج إلى سبب غير فطري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted object of Satan’s enmity is Adam and his descendants.
rows.anchor: أي عدو لآدم وذرية آدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Manifest” modifies “misleading,” rather than serving as a second or third predicate.
rows.anchor: لا خبر ثان ولا ثالث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next statement substitutes for the whole prior sentence: recognizing Satan’s deception entails seeing the act as self-wrong, confessing the error, and asking God’s forgiveness.
rows.anchor: لأن الجزم بكون ما صدر منه عملا من عمل الشيطان وتغريره يشتمل على أن ذلك ظلم لنفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses called the act self-wrong because anger on behalf of his partisan made him strike too soon when he could have controlled himself; he calls it misguidance in 26:20.
rows.anchor: لأنه كان من أثر فرط الغضب لأجل رجل من شيعته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ wrong exposed him to the Copts’ plotting to kill him and exceeded the Egyptian’s offense with disproportionate punishment.
rows.anchor: أنه تسبب لنفسه في مضرة إضمار القبط قتله

rows.speaker: وداك بن ثميل المازني
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr suggests Moses may not have investigated which combatant was wrong, describing this as tribal partisanship; he quotes Waddāk praising his people for aiding allies without asking who summoned them or why.
rows.anchor: كما قال وداك بن ثميل المازني يمدح قومه : إذا استنجدوا لم يسألوا من دعاهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses reached this moral understanding by inspiration, since the Egyptians then had no divine law; alternatively, he may have learned it from his mother and people, who retained elements of Isaac’s and Jacob’s religion.
rows.anchor: إذ لم تكن يومئذ شريعة إلهية في القبط . ويجوز أن يكون علمه بذلك مما تلقاه من أمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: There is no issue of a prophet sinning here because Moses was not yet a prophet.
rows.anchor: ولا التفات في هذا إلى جواز صدور الذنب من النبي لأنه لم يكن يومئذ نبيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question of pre-prophethood sin concerns acts already prohibited by that prophet’s own law or a law he followed, as with Jesus under the Torah before his mission.
rows.anchor: لأن تلك مفروضة فيما تقرر حكمه من الذنوب بحسب شرع ذلك النبي أو شرع نبيء هو متبعه مثل عيسى عليه السلام قبل نبوءته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fāʾ in “He forgave him” marks immediate succession: God answered Moses’ plea promptly with forgiveness.
rows.anchor: أي استجاب استغفاره فعجل له بالمغفرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The forgiveness clause is parenthetical between Moses’ confession and vow, informing Qur’an readers of Moses’ honored standing with God.
rows.anchor: كان اعتراضها إعلاما لأهل القرآن بكرامة موسى عليه السلام عند ربه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “He is the Forgiving, the Merciful” explains the forgiveness; its emphatic restriction gestures to the specific self-wrong and circumstances described.
rows.anchor: علل المغفرة له بأنه شديد الغفران ورحيم بعباده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating “he said” emphasizes and reconnects Moses’ speech after the intervening forgiveness statement; the vow is not a response to forgiveness because Moses had not been told it occurred.
rows.anchor: أعيد القول للتنبيه على اتصال كلام موسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bāʾ in “for what You favored me” expresses cause; mā is relative with a commonly omitted pronoun governed by the same preposition, though it may instead be a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: موصولة وحذف العائد من الصلة لأنه ضمير مجرور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The favor may mean wisdom and knowledge that disclosed realities beyond customs, leading Moses to refuse support for criminals.
rows.anchor: هو ما أوتيه من الحكمة والعلم فتميزت عنده الحقائق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By criminals Moses meant those he recognized as oppressors who humiliated people, like the Copt forcing the Israelite to carry wood.
rows.anchor: وأراد بهم الذين يستذلون الناس ويظلمونهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses may have offered the vow as reflection on the killing, confident that he had killed the Copt unintentionally.
rows.anchor: ولعل هذا الكلام ساقه مساق الاعتبار عن قتله القبطي وثوقا بأنه قتله خطأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fāʾ connects the vow as a consequence of the relative clause, which often behaves like a conditional, especially when a fronted genitive carries that force; Ibn ʿĀshūr cites a hadith construction as analogy.
rows.anchor: بالفاء لأن الموصول كثيرا ما يعامل معاملة اسم الشرط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ẓahīr means helper or supporter.
rows.anchor: وإعطائه جوابا مجزوما . والظهير : النصير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses makes refusing to support criminals the return for wisdom and knowledge: gratitude means defending truth and changing wrong, since tolerating evil colludes with its doer.
rows.anchor: وقد دل هذا النظم على أن موسى أراد أن يجعل عدم مظاهرته للمجرمين جزاء على نعمة الحكمة والعلم بأن جعل شكر تلك النعمة الانتصار للحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ next-day effort to strike another Copt fulfills his vow: the Copt was an idolater and the Israelite a monotheist.
rows.anchor: ومما يؤيد هذا التفسير أن موسى لما أصبح من الغد فوجد الرجل الذي استصرخه في أمسه يستصرخه على قبطي آخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority of the early authorities treated this verse as evidence against assisting unjust rulers in any matter; God recounts Moses’ vow approvingly as true speech.
rows.anchor: وقد جعل جمهور من السلف هذه الآية حجة على منع إعانة أهل الجور في شيء من أمورهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s transcendence is qualified by what polytheists associate because they alone attribute impossible or unworthy things to Him, such as a son, claim He commanded their shameful customs, or treat idols as intercessors; others acknowledge His perfection.
rows.anchor: أنه لم يجترىء أحد أن يصف الله تعالى بما لا يليق به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mā in this clause is a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: مصدرية أي سبحانه وتعالى عن إشراكهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 69 continues from God’s creating and choosing: He fashioned people so their beliefs and deeds arise from them, with readiness for good or evil, while He knows what they conceal and declare.
rows.anchor: هو خالقهم ومركبهم على النظام الذي تصدر عنه الأفعال والاعتقادات فيكونون مستعدين لقبول الخير والشر وتغليب أحدهما على الآخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun “their breasts” refers to the creatures denoted by “whatever He wills”; rational pronouns show that humans are intended by the general expression.
rows.anchor: أي ما تكن صدور المخلوقات وما يعلنون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God selects and requites people according to what He knows of them, implying the rationale for choice and the promise and threat; this is highly compressed expression.
rows.anchor: فبحسب ما يعلم منهم يختارهم ويجازيهم فحصل بهذا إيماء إلى علة الاختيار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Addressing God as “your Lord” hints that their hidden thoughts include hatred of Muhammad, as noted at the end of Sūrat al-Naml.
rows.anchor: إيماء إلى أن مما تكنه صدورهم بغض محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 70 continues the account of creation and choice; its main point is that judgment belongs to God, with the preceding description proving His exclusive rule and embedding His majesty.
rows.anchor: وإنما قدم عليه ما هو دليل على أنه المنفرد بالحكم مع إدماج صفات عظمته الذاتية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening pronoun refers back to the One described from 28:58 onward, and the divine name is its predicate; this prevents confusion or assigning the name’s qualities elsewhere.
rows.anchor: أي الموصوف بتلك الصفات العظيمة والفاعل لتلك الأفعال الجليلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “There is no god but Him” further establishes that the named God alone is truly divine; polytheists wrongly assign divinity to idols, so the statement refutes shirk after its eschatological exposure in 28:64.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا الخبر الثاني زيادة تقرير لمدلول الخبر الأول فإن اسم الجلالة اختص بالدلالة على الإله الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Exclusive praise in both abodes proves no other is divine: even polytheists praise only God; the lām denotes possession, fronting gives true exclusivity, and generic al-ḥamd encompasses all praise.
rows.anchor: وهو استدلال على انتفاء إلهية غيره بحجة أن الناس مؤمنهم وكافرهم لا يحمدون في الدنيا إلا الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ūlā means this world, where praise of others is figurative; the verse’s afterlife praise is genuine and is illustrated by 17:52.
rows.anchor: هي الدنيا وتخصيص الحمد به في الدنيا اختصاص لجنس الحمد به لأن حمد غيره مجاز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “To Him belongs judgment” uses possession and fronting for exclusivity; judgment is assigning benefit or harm, with its object understood as both abodes. Other worldly judgment is figurative, while judgment in the afterlife belongs only to God, refuting idols and their alleged intercession.
rows.anchor: وحذف المتعلق بالحكم لدلالة قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “To Him you return” specifies afterlife return after the general mention of all praise and judgment: people will glorify Him and undergo His rule, obliging them to affirm resurrection.
rows.anchor: أي أنكم ترجعون إليه في الآخرة فتمجدونه ويجري عليكم حكمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fronted “to Him” serves the rhyme and emphasizes the final arrival at His judgment.
rows.anchor: للرعاية على الفاصلة وللاهتمام بالانتهاء إليه أي إلى حكمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discourse shifts from proving God’s uniqueness through His attributes to His crafted signs, while embedding gratitude for blessings and censuring polytheist ingratitude.
rows.anchor: انتقال من الاستدلال على انفراده تعالى بالإلهية بصفات ذاته إلى الاستدلال على ذلك ببديع مصنوعاته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alternating day and night, repeated twice daily and perceptible to everyone, is an evident proof of origination; even idols change between darkness and light.
rows.anchor: والذي هو أجلى مظاهر التغير في هذا العالم فهو دليل الحدوث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternating opposites demonstrates power more clearly than one permanent state, and the changing blessings are more valuable than one fixed condition; the alternation itself suffices even if people miss each sign’s wisdom.
rows.anchor: لأن قدرة خالق الضدين وجاعل أحدهما ينسخ الآخر كل يوم أظهر منها لو لم يخلق إلا أقواهما وأنفعهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the earth’s sprouting life and its barrenness death is metaphorical.
rows.anchor: وأطلق على إنبات الأرض إحياء وعلى قحولتها الموت على سبيل الاستعارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that God revives the dead resumes the argument and inserts proof of resurrection after reflection on the earth’s revival; the emphatic particle also conveys causal “so,” as in Bashshār’s verse.
rows.anchor: استئناف وهو إدماج ؛ أدمج دليل البعث عقب الاعتبار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demonstrative points to God described as reviving the earth, so the One who revives it is worthy of the following predicate; pointing is concise and exalted compared with a relative clause.
rows.anchor: واسم الإشارة عائد إلى اسم الله تعالى بما أجري عليه من الإخبار بإحياء الأرض بعد موتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s power over everything includes resurrection, which is bringing creatures into existence as He created them the first time.
rows.anchor: فإنه يعم جميع الأشياء والبعث من جملتها إذ ليس هو إلا إيجاد خلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The analogy is exact: reviving the earth creates likenesses of its former plants, just as resurrection creates likenesses of the dead.
rows.anchor: لأن إحياء الأرض إيجاد أمثال ما كان عليها من النبات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, and Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim read the word in the singular; the other readers use the plural.
rows.anchor: وقرأ نافع وابن كثير وأبو عمرو وأبو بكر عن عاصم { إلى أثر } بالإفراد .

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The following sentence connects to 30:49 after an intervening excursus and depicts ingrained ingratitude: people rejoice at blessing without thanks, then lapse into despair when wind scorches promising green crops.
rows.anchor: وهذه الجملة سيقت للتنبيه على أن الكفران مطبوع في نفوسهم بحيث يعاودهم بأدنى سبب فهم إذا أصابتهم النعمة استبشروا ولم يشكروا
